en: The Sutra on the Threefold Recitation of Impermanence Spoken by the Buddha.
May those who practice all reach the shore of the unconditioned (*asamskrta*).
The Dharma-cloud and Dharma-rain nourish all living beings; They can eliminate feverish afflictions and purge all maladies.
They bring those who are difficult to transform to harmony and compliance, guiding them according to their capacities rather than through forceful means.
I bow my head in refuge to the True Assembly of Noble Ones—the eight classes of superiors who have been able to leave defilement behind.
With the vajra-wisdom mallet, they shatter the mountains of heterodoxy, forever severing the entanglements of beginningless time.

From the Deer Park to the Twin Trees, following the Buddha throughout his lifetime as he propagated the True Teaching, each according to their original conditions and having completed their transformative work, they extinguished their bodies and ceased their wisdom to realize non-arising.
I bow my head in universal reverence to the Honored Ones of the Triple Gem; this is called the Right Cause that can universally save.
Deluded and ignorant, beings are perpetually submerged in birth and death; may all be caused to emerge and reach Bodhi.
All who are born must return to death; their countenances utterly change and decay. When powerful disease invades, none can escape this fate.
Even if it were Mount Sumeru, at the end of the kalpa, it would all be scattered and destroyed.
The great ocean, deep and bottomless, shall likewise be completely exhausted; the great earth, the sun, and the moon, when their time comes, all return to extinction.
There has never been a single thing that has not been swallowed by impermanence.
Even those reborn in non-human realms, down to the universal monarchs whose seven treasures always follow them—none escape.
Surrounded constantly by a thousand sons, yet when their lifespan is exhausted, they do not pause for even a moment;
they drift once more into the sea of death, undergoing manifold sufferings according to conditions.
Circling within the three realms like a water-wheel drawing from a well, they are also like silkworms making cocoons, spinning threads that bind themselves.
Even the Unsurpassed World-Honored Ones, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas, must relinquish their impermanent bodies;

how much more so for ordinary people? Parents, wives and children, brothers, and kinsmen—when one witnesses them separated by the barrier of birth and death, how could one not grieve and lament? Therefore, I exhort you, my sons.
Listen attentively to the true Dharma; together, abandon the realm of impermanence. You should practice the gateway to the deathless.
The Buddha’s teaching is like nectar: it removes fever and brings cooling refreshment. Listen well with a single mind;
it can extinguish all afflictions. Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are three kinds of dharmas."
In all the worlds, this is unlovely;
this is lacking in luster.
This is not to be contemplated;
this is not to one's liking. What are the three?
That is to say: old age, sickness, and death.
O bhikṣus, this is old age, sickness, and death.
In all the worlds,
they are truly not lovely;
they are truly not radiant.
It is truly not worth contemplating;
it is truly not to one's liking.
If old age, sickness, and death did not exist in this world, [it would be so].

If the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha did not appear in the world to teach sentient beings the Dharma he has realized and the matters of discipline, one would not know this aging, illness, and death.
Therefore, it should be known that [these exist].
In all the worlds, this is unlovely;
this is lacking in luster.
This is not to be contemplated; this is not to be approved.
By these three matters.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,
has appeared in the world to teach sentient beings the Dharma he has realized and the matters of discipline.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again:
External affairs, fine robes, and all such things come to ruin; internal decay and transformation of the body are likewise the same.
Only the supreme Dharma does not perish; therefore, those with wisdom should carefully examine this.
Old age, sickness, and death are universally loathed; the physical form becomes ugly and extremely repulsive.
The youthful appearance remains but for a moment; before long, all shall become withered and decayed.
Even if one’s lifespan were to reach a full hundred years, in the end one cannot escape the pressure of impermanence.
The sufferings of old age, illness, and death constantly follow, always bringing no benefit to sentient beings.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking this sutra,
the assembly of bhikṣus, along with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and others,
were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
Constantly seeking the objects of desire, one does not practice virtuous deeds.

How can one preserve the body and life when death is seen to invade? When the life-faculty, breath, and desires are exhausted, and all the limbs are severed, suffering accompanies death; at that time, lamenting in vain, both eyes roll upward.
The sword of death descends according to one's karma; Thoughts and perceptions are simultaneously filled with terror.
No one can provide rescue or relief; Long gasps for breath cause the chest to tighten in urgency. The breath is stifled, the throat becomes parched;
King Death urges on the Lord of Life (Yama), While relatives stand by in vain. All consciousnesses grow dark and obscured, As one enters the perilous city.
Relatives and friends all abandon him; He is dragged away by the Black Rope Hell-hounds.
Led before King Yama, he receives retribution according to his karma: Through superior causes one is born in the good realms; Through evil karma one falls into hell.
No vision surpasses wisdom; No darkness exceeds ignorance; No illness is greater than enmity.
Nothing is more terrifying than death; all who are born must inevitably die. Having committed sins, one suffers in the body;
therefore, one should diligently exert the three karmas, constantly cultivating merit and wisdom. One’s kin and retinue will all be abandoned, and one’s wealth and goods will be taken by others;
one carries only one’s own roots of goodness as provisions for the perilous path.
Just as a tree by the roadside provides a brief rest but not a long stay, so too are chariots, horses, wives, and children;

none endure for long. Like a flock of birds that roost together at night and fly apart at dawn, so too is the separation from kinsmen and acquaintances upon death. Only the Buddha’s awakening remains.
This is the true refuge; based on the sutras, I have briefly explained it. Wise ones should reflect upon this well.

May the devas, asuras, yakṣas, and others who come to listen to the Dharma, with sincere hearts, protect the Buddha-dharma so that it may endure forever, and each diligently practice the teachings of the World-Honored One.
All you disciples who have come here, whether dwelling upon the earth or abiding in the sky,
may you always give rise to a heart of compassion for the human world; may you abide according to the Dharma throughout day and night,
and may all worlds be forever peaceful and secure, benefiting all living beings with boundless merit and wisdom.
All karmic obscurations and misdeeds are completely eliminated; Free from all suffering, one returns to parinirvāṇa.

Constantly anointing the body with the fragrance of ethical discipline, And always wearing the robes of meditative concentration to sustain the self, Adorned everywhere with the exquisite flowers of bodhi, One dwells in constant peace and happiness wherever one stays.

The *Buddhabhāṣita-anityatā-triskandha-sūtra*, one fascicle. The initial and concluding praises were compiled by the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa based on the meaning of the sūtra; the central portion is the authentic scripture spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth. Because the subject matter is divided into three sections, it is called the "Three-Sectioned Sūtra" (*Triskandha*).
